hook: SCP-165 is a Keter-class swarm, and the article asks you to picture it at two scales at once: a single mite under the microscope and a sand dune big enough to flood a building. The first half is a dry biology report; the second turns into a frontier ghost story set in the Arizona desert. It is a quick, nasty creature feature with a history attached.
whyItMatters: Its threat is built from ordinary biology pushed to absurd numbers: mites much like house dust mites, a numbing bite like a mosquito's, and hundreds of billions of individuals. Nothing about one animal is supernatural, which is why the containment logic of heat, microwave fields and scheduled cattle feels believable. It is also a good example of an acquisition addendum carrying most of an article's atmosphere.
thingsToNotice:
The real horror is the anaesthetic. Because the bite numbs, a sleeping animal can have a limb stripped to the bone in minutes without waking, while the swarm spins around it like a vortex and millions of mites take turns tearing off mouthfuls. The article is careful to say they compete rather than cooperate, setting them against an expunged colony organism that does show a group mind.

The history comes in layers: a German immigrant town emptied by 1908, a cavalry troop that loses seven horses to bone piles in one night and four soldiers who are never seen again, a bombing range set up in the late 1950s to wipe the mites out, and a 1980s task force that glasses the sand with flame. The old warning sign about hungry, creeping sand is the only voice left from the settlers. Nearly four tonnes of the dune survived and still have to be fed a whole cow every nine days.
